members.title: 踏火猎金！《雾影猎人》S2 赛季更新，咪咕游戏开启双十一福利

news.body:
由咪咕游戏独家发行的《雾影猎人》S2赛季「旧日之火」正式上线，全新玩法、武器流派、主线剧情及多项优化同步推出。咪咕游戏双十一促销开启，标准版仅68元、豪华版99元。限时福利与S2赛季列锋电竞赛招募同步展开，邀请新老玩家组队猎金。
业火争锋上线，全新玩法与BOSS同步登场
S2赛季全新玩法「业火争锋」登场，随机出现的业火禁地将改变地图环境。玩家在区域内持续积累灼热值，达到上限后进入「狂焰」状态，持续掉血，只有使用冷饮或在稻草人处祈祷才可以消除灼热值。
玩家还将迎战全新BOSS昔日曜日祭司·拉尔斯，通过主线剧情探寻灾厄背后的真相。黑箭解锁第二武器流派「投矛」，兼顾近战与远程攻击。为投矛灌注神力可强化攻击，搭配「矛无虚发」天赋，神力状态下的投矛可自动追踪准心附近的目标。本赛季同步上线「灵魂烙印」成长系统与契约时装，并优化任务要求、提高奖励，减轻玩家养成负担。
咪咕游戏双十一回馈价来袭，专属福利同步上线
咪咕游戏本次双十一促销，《雾影猎人》标准版仅68元、豪华版99元。玩家还可在直播间享受专属优惠，标准版66元、豪华版98元。咪咕游戏客户端内同步上线限时福利活动。玩家完成登录、社区互动、游玩打卡及签到等任务，即可收集碎片参与抽奖，赢取PS5手柄、《雾影猎人》CDKEY、咪咕游戏VIP月卡及游戏礼包等奖励。三人组队猎金，还可参与开箱活动。
列锋赛启幕，高手竞逐等你报名
11月11日正式启动2026《雾影猎人》列锋电竞赛，并于咪咕游戏内启动招募，设置高校选拔赛、全网线上赛两大赛道，面向各路高手与高校玩家征集选手，经海选最终决出6名线上选手与2名高校选手，共8人晋级线下全国总决赛。赛事将选用专属OB竞赛房进行比赛，采用创新赛点积分赛制，根据物资带出、击杀玩家、特殊宝箱与BOSS成就等维度综合核算积分，多维度规则让赛场对抗充满悬念。

news.summary_raw: 索尼互动娱乐于今日宣布，蒙特利尔 Haven 工作室研发的在线服务型射击游戏《Fairgame$ 》正式取消。展望未来，工作室将把重心转向协助 PlayStation 工作室的其他团队，同时探索新的创作机会。 据悉，本次游戏取消不会引发工作室裁员。高管 Sean Decker 与 John Doyle 表示，近期一场数千名玩家参与的测试未达到预期。虽然测试展现了出色的运营准备与社区参与度，但玩家反馈和留存率不及预期。结合 PVP 射击游戏市场的严峻环境，索尼做出了艰难的决定。 作为一款“搜打撤”游戏，《Fairgame$》于2023年首次公布。该项目在过去3年里经历过多次重组与修改，工作室原本计划以全新的名称在发布会上重新亮相。索尼此前曾计划推出十多款在线服务型游戏，但在诸多惨败后决定大幅收缩。

members.title: 独立游戏节IGF部分评委强烈抵制AI游戏，《Big Walk》或无缘评选
House House clarifies use of AI tools in Big Walk's "final stage of development"

news.body:
包括 Sam Barlow 与 Austin Walker 在内的19名2027年独立游戏节 IGF 评委联合于日前发表声明，宣布拒绝为任何使用生成式 AI 制作的游戏投票。这些评委呼吁 IGF 能够制定严格政策，全面禁止包含 AI 生成内容的作品参选。
根据这些评委的说法，做出这一决定是为了声援对行业前景感到担忧的创作者。他们认为，生成式 AI 会在生态、经济、认知及劳动权益等多个层面带来负面影响，这种伤害涵盖图像、音效、代码等所有环节。不仅用于训练模型的历史作品没有获得原作者授权，包括编程劳动在内的所有工作也应当得到同等尊重。这些评委更是表示，有其他评委出于职业风险等方面的顾虑而没有参与联署。
随着事件发酵，House House 工作室开发的《Big Walk》也确认成为了他们的抵制对象。House House 则回应称，项目后期曾使用 LLM 解决性能问题，但仅限于辅助技术排查。AI 生成的内容占游戏总代码不到 0.1%，其他创作环节均未使用。
开发团队同时表示，支持限制生成式 AI 危害的努力，也承认此前没有建立内部规范是自己的失误。由于V社豁免了 AI 辅助编码等用途的披露，《Big Walk》的商店页面确实没有相关说明。鉴于这些评委决定抵制任何有 AI 参与的游戏，这款广受好评的作品很可能也将无缘 IGF。

news.summary_raw: The game will be delisted from stores in November, and the servers will go offline in May.

members.title: Ratchet & Clank: Ranger Rumble Is Shutting Down a Year After Its Soft Launch
PlayStation cancels Ratchet & Clank: Ranger Rumble a year into soft launch

news.body:
Ratchet & Clank: Ranger Rumble Is Shutting Down a Year After Its Soft Launch
The game will be delisted from stores in November, and the servers will go offline in May.
Ratchet & Clank: Ranger Rumble, a free multiplayer shooter for Android and iOS, will be delisted later in November and shut down next May.
In a statement on the game's official website, PlayStation said it would stop developing the title. The final planned update rolled out on the App Store and Google Play on November 6, and no further updates are planned.
The app will be removed from stores and no longer available to download on November 21. Players who have already installed the game can play it until May 1, 2027, with all current game modes, matchmaking, and competitive features. In May, the game's servers will shut down permanently, and all player data will be deleted.
In-game purchases have also been removed. Players can keep earning rewards through play and spend the in-game currency they earn on upgrades, cosmetics, characters, and other currencies. The Qwark Pass seasons will run until May 1, and the Super Pass is now free, with all of its content earnable throughout each season. Other Ratchet & Clank games and PlayStation services are not affected by the end of the game’s development. The announcement comes with an FAQ explaining how players can use the game's features during the transition period.
"On behalf of the dev team and everyone helping to make the game, thanks to our amazing community for all your support, especially to those who have spent time playing, sharing feedback, and helping shape Ranger Rumble throughout its development!" the statement reads.
Oh BiBi, Insomniac Games, Sony Interactive Entertainment
Ratchet & Clank: Ranger Rumble was developed by the French studio Oh BiBi in collaboration with PlayStation Studios and Insomniac Games. The game first soft-launched in the Philippines and Indonesia in November 2025, and then expanded to more countries, including Norway, Sweden, Finland, Denmark, France, Canada, and the UK. This July, Sony announced plans for its global launch and opened pre-registration. However, the game never launched globally.
Ratchet & Clank, a series of action-adventure platformers and third-person shooters, was created by Insomniac Games. The first game was released in 2002 for PlayStation 2, and many more titles followed. Apart from Ranger Rumble, the series features three mobile titles: the 2005 Ratchet & Clank: Going Mobile; Ratchet & Clank: Clone Home, released a year later; and the 2013 Ratchet & Clank: Before the Nexus.

news.title: 10 teams, 3 programs, and 7 years: Efficiently managing 3D assets in defense training
news.summary_raw: i3 Corps maintains military digital twins for years. See how its 10 art teams manage 3D assets with Unity Addressables and Unity Asset Manager.

members.title: 10 teams, 3 programs, and 7 years: Efficiently managing 3D assets in defense training

news.body:
10 teams, 3 programs, and 7 years: Efficiently managing 3D assets in defense training
This guest post comes from Daniel Starkey, Marketing Director, and John Thornton, Systems Architect, at i3 Corps. They build virtual training and engineering productivity tools for US government customers, and here Daniel and John explain what a decade of military digital twins does to a 3D asset pipeline.
i3 Corps builds virtual training and engineering productivity tools for government customers. Over the years we have developed hundreds of training scenarios in Unity, covering most of the aviation training we support, along with Navy platforms and ground vehicles. Those applications reach classrooms on military installations across the country through a government-owned distribution platform we built, running in a secure government cloud.
The applications are the visible part. The hard part sits underneath them, in the 3D library, and almost none of the standard advice about asset pipelines carries through.
A model that outlives the program that bought it
In most 3D work, an asset is finished when the product ships.
Our models are digital twins of physical equipment, and the physical equipment keeps changing. A new component enters service. A manufacturer revises a part. A customer sends a fresh CAD package, and the model has to absorb it. One of our aircraft models runs to 80,000 components, down to the nuts and bolts. We add ten to fifteen new models a year, and each one starts a maintenance relationship that can run eight or nine years.
That creates a problem most pipelines never have to solve. When new engineering data arrives, someone has to work out what it changes. Which parts does it supersede? Which existing model does it update? Which of the applications already in classrooms depend on that model, and what happens to them?
The reference data compounds the same way. Our models are built from CAD packages from different sources and from photogrammetry we capture ourselves. A single capture trip can produce millions of photographs of one vehicle. Years later, when new CAD arrives for the same platform, you need to know where the original model came from, so you can compare the two. That answer is easy to lose and expensive to reconstruct.
Same airframe, different aircraft
Take the UH-60 Black Hawk. The US Army alone flies a long list of versions: the UH-60A, L, M, and V, the HH-60M MEDEVAC, and specialized aircraft for special operations and other missions. Add the Navy, the Air Force, and international operators, and the number of configurations someone needs to train on grows fast.
Every one of them is a legitimate training target, but they aren't separate aircraft. Most share the same fuselage, tail boom, rotor assemblies, and landing gear. The UH-60V keeps much of the L's airframe and adds a digital cockpit. The HH-60M MEDEVAC is built on the UH-60M, with medical equipment and mission systems added.
Model each one from scratch and you're rebuilding, revalidating, and maintaining the same parts over and over. The better approach is a common baseline built from reusable components, where each variant adds only what's actually different: structure, mechanical systems, avionics, or mission equipment.
Explore every angle of the aircraft.
The last mile is a ten-year-old computer
Consumer software deals with storage pressure by ignoring it. It downloads tens of gigabytes and expects you to delete something else to make room.
We can’t do that. Our applications land on government machines that may be older, carry significant security controls, and have firm limits on how much space anyone can use. A classroom machine might hold every training course we have ever built for that platform. Compiled the conventional way, with models baked into each application, that’s hundreds of gigabytes of largely identical geometry.
We use Unity Addressables to avoid that. Models live in a catalog rather than inside the build, they’re pulled on demand, and they are cached locally. Deduplication is the default rather than an optimization, because an asset referenced by fifteen applications is stored once. Applications only need to change when their code changes. It also means a developer does not need the entire library on one machine to assemble a scene.
Security is also a critical factor. Classified material never touches the cloud, Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI) can, but it needs to be wrapped so nobody can open the model on the machine and walk out with it. Knowing which category an asset falls into, reliably and at a glance, is not administrative overhead. It determines where the asset is allowed to exist.
A related question comes up constantly and has nothing to do with security: who owns this? Some assets are i3 property, and some are government property, and the distinction determines whether we can reuse an asset on the next contract, or reference it in a proposal.
Why we stopped building our own catalog
We’d started building one.
For a long time there was no government-cloud option for this kind of tooling, so we surveyed the commercial asset management platforms and kept hitting the same two problems: either the tool didn’t fit how our data actually works, or the licensing model made it impractical for government use. So we began assembling our own, layering a database and search on top of our existing version control and automation.
It worked, up to a point. We could find assets. What we could not justify was the rest: the engine integration, the pipeline automation, the dependency tracking, and then maintaining it all indefinitely.
That’s not our business. We deliver training and engineering solutions to government customers, and a toolchain our artists and developers can use without leaving Unity is worth more to us than a bespoke system we’d have to keep alive ourselves.
That is why we deployed Unity Asset Manager into a government cloud environment, and why we’re now working with Unity on what it needs to become for pipelines like ours.
What we’re solving next
Cataloging finished assets is the first step, and it already answers questions we used to answer by asking around. What have we modeled? Where is it used? Is it controlled? Who owns it?
The harder problem is volatility. Our catalog is not a shelf of finished work. Ten art teams change assets weekly, sometimes daily, for years, and every change ripples through long dependency chains built for complex maintenance animations. Managing that well means telling artists precisely what changed, rather than reversioning everything downstream of it.
That is the work in front of us, and we will write about it as we go, including the parts that are not solved yet.
There is a larger reason to get it right. The government owns enormous quantities of CAD and parametric model data, much of it delivered under contract years ago and effectively unfindable now. Meanwhile the demand is shifting from training alone toward simulation, visualization, and AI-assisted content generation, all of which need a searchable library of accurate 3D data underneath. A model is only useful if you can find it. Increasingly, it’s only useful if a machine can find it too.
In an upcoming article we will get specific about that work, including where Unity Asset Manager doesn’t yet fit a pipeline like ours and what we and Unity are building together to close the gap.
We will also be at I/ITSEC 2026 in Orlando, November 30 to December 3, booth #1761. Come find us.

news.title: 10 tips for organizing your first video game project with AI
news.summary_raw: How to organize a video game project with AI: 10 beginner tips on design briefs, naming, checkpoints, prompt logs, and playtesting – no coding needed.

members.title: 10 tips for organizing your first video game project with AI

news.body:
10 tips for organizing your first video game project with AI
Unity Team - Unity Technologies
Keep your first video game on track from day one with ten simple ways to organize your ideas, prompts, and progress.
Think about the last time you asked someone for something, got a result you almost liked, and then couldn’t remember exactly what you asked. Now picture that happening across every character, screen, and rule in a video game. That’s what organizing a game project means: deciding what you’re building, what each piece is called, and how you keep track of changes, ideas, and progress.
When you build a game with AI by prompting a tool like Unity Spark to create it (or vibe code it) from a plain-language description, you don’t need to write code or learn a traditional game engine.
You still make the decisions an engine normally forces on you, though: what each screen does, how everything looks, and what to build next. These ten habits keep those decisions in one place. They don’t take technical skills, and they’ll save you time whether you’re working alone or with friends.
1. Write one design brief and keep it handy
Open any notes app and start one page that describes your game. Begin with a single sentence about what the player does, like “The player guides a moth through a dark garden to collect glowing lights while dodging bats.” That sentence names your core game loop, the action players repeat most. Then add the controls, how a player wins and loses, and the look you want.
This brief is your home base, and it doubles as the source for your first prompt. When you’re unsure what to ask for next, start there. Our one-page design document guide has a template you can copy into your notes.
2. Build one small piece at a time
A whole game is a lot to ask for in one go, and a long request is harder to check. Split your game into pieces you can finish one at a time: a title screen, level one, a win screen, a lose screen. Ask for one piece, look at what you get, and fix it before you move on. When something goes wrong, you’ll know where to look, because you only changed one thing.
List your pieces in your notes and work through them in order. Finishing a small piece feels good, and it keeps the project moving.
3. Name things once, and use the same word every time
Names keep you and your tools on the same page. Pick one name for each character, object, and screen, write it in your notes, and use exactly that word every time you describe it. If your main character is “Moth,” don’t call it “the player,” “my bug,” and “the little guy” in different requests. Different words can read as different things, so your results may drift. If you rename something later, update your notes and use the new name everywhere.
4. Keep one list for all your ideas
New ideas will keep coming, and when adding a feature is as easy as typing a request, it’s tempting to say yes to all of them. Keep a single ideas list in your notes and sort each idea under one heading: must have, should have, could have, or won’t have this time. To decide, ask, “What happens if this is missing?” If the answer is “The game doesn’t work,” it’s a must-have.
For the moth game, moth movement, collectible lights, and moving bats are must-haves, because without them there’s no game. Story cutscenes (short, movie-like scenes that play without the player controlling anything) and online leaderboards (a ranking list that shows the highest scores from players around the world) go under won’t have. Both are nice to have, but the game works without them, and each one takes extra time to build. Keeping the won’ts on the list, instead of deleting them, stops cut ideas from sneaking back in and gives you a head start on your next game.
5. Describe your look in words you can reuse
A game looks best when everything in it matches, and a tool can only match what you describe. Write a short style description in your notes: the visual style you chose, such as pixel art or hand-drawn, your color palette, the shapes you’ll use for friendly and dangerous characters, and a few reference images. Studios call this an art bible. Yours can be a few lines.
Then reuse those exact words in your requests, so each new screen or character comes out matching the last.
6. Change one thing at a time, then playtest
When you ask for several changes at once, it’s hard to tell which one caused a problem. Ask for one change, play your game for a minute, and decide whether to keep it or undo it. Small and frequent beats big and surprising.
Playing matters more than it seems. There’s always a gap between how you imagine a game will feel and how it plays in practice, so play after every change instead of every few.
7. Save a checkpoint before big changes
Professional teams use software called version control, a system that records the history of a project so they can go back if something goes wrong. Spark has a version of that habit built in. It saves a restore point automatically after each prompt, and restoring one puts your whole game back to that point. A restore is recorded as a new entry in your history, so you can undo it by restoring to just before it. For small fixes, undo and redo (Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Shift+Z) step back through recent edits one at a time.
Restore points don’t last forever. Spark keeps them for 7 days, and only the newest 20 in each conversation, so very old history may not be restorable. Before a big change, write a short label in your notes for the version you’d want to come back to and the request it followed, such as “v3 – added bats, after request 7.” Unity’s guidance recommends small, frequent saves with clear descriptions, and says these habits are useful even on a solo project.
8. Keep a prompt log
In your notes, keep a running log of what you asked and what happened. For each request, write the request, what you got, and whether you kept it. For example: “Request 7: add three bats that fly across the garden. Result: bats appear but fly too fast. Next: ask for slower bats.”
A log lets you repeat what worked, avoid what didn’t, and pick up where you left off after a break. Over time, it also shows you which kinds of requests give you the results you want.
9. Keep track of where things came from
If your tool lets you upload your own images or sounds or creates art and music for you, note where each piece came from: made by you, created by the tool, or downloaded from someone else. For anything from outside, write down who made it and what the terms say, including whether it needs a credit and whether you can use it in a game you share. That way you always know what’s yours, what came from elsewhere, and what you might need to credit.
10. Track what’s done and what’s left
A project without a finish line never ends, and without a list of what’s left, it’s hard to tell how close you are. Make a simple tracker with three columns: to do, doing, and done. Start by filling the first column with what finished means for this version. A simple checklist might include:
- A title screen
- Your core gameplay
- A way to win or lose
- Sound effects
- A score or other way to track progress
- A version you can share
Move items across as you finish them, and add three or four milestones with rough dates, like “playable core gameplay” and “shared with friends.” Show your game to real people as soon as it’s playable, even if it’s rough.
Your turn
Open your notes app and write your one-sentence game description. Fill in this sentence:
In my game, you ___, then ___, so you can ___.
Save it as the first line of your design brief. That’s a project with a home, and every other habit on this list builds from there. When you get access to Unity Spark, paste it in as your first prompt, play what you get, and write down the first thing you’d change.
Ready to try organizing your first video game project? You don’t need to be a developer. Try Unity Spark, Unity’s browser-based, AI game creation platform that allows you to describe your game, refine it in a real web editor, and publish it for others to play.

members.title: TCL敢为不凡杯全球高校电子竞技联赛S5总决赛圆满收官

news.body:
11月7日，TCL敢为不凡杯全球高校电子竞技联赛S5总决赛在西安曲江WE电子竞技俱乐部主场馆顺利落幕。该场馆同时也是 TCL 敢为不凡杯 S3 总决赛的举办地，来自全国各地的高校选手和观众再度在这里见证高校电竞荣耀诞生。
本赛季 TCL 敢为不凡杯共有 2077 支战队参赛，总参与人次超 1.25 万，985、211 等重点高校选手占比 50%。赛事首次设置南北两大赛区，采用跨校混战模式，一改往届校内先行对战的形式，开赛就是校际激烈交锋。校园赛期间，TCL 联动各校电竞社，保障赛事专业落地。对比前几届，本届赛事规模更大、赛制更专业、赛程更具看点。
本次总决赛设置英雄联盟、无畏契约两大赛道，英雄联盟赛道由武汉大学 WHU 战队对阵华南师范大学 SCNU 战队，无畏契约赛道则由成都大学成都狂少战队迎战南京传媒学院 CUCN 战队。多轮激烈博弈过后，成都狂少战队拿下无畏契约赛道冠军，南京传媒学院 CUCN 战队获得该赛道亚军。
英雄联盟赛道的冠军由武汉大学 WHU 战队斩获，华南师范大学 SCNU 战队收获亚军。这一冠，是武汉大学跨越四年的圆梦时刻。2023 年，队伍首次登上 TCL 敢为不凡杯赛场，未能走到最后；2024 年，同样在西安曲江电竞中心，武大战队遗憾不敌深圳大学，与冠军失之交臂；2025 年，队伍止步晋级赛，再度抱憾离场；2026 年，即将毕业的队员迎来属于自己的最后一舞，带着四年的不甘与积淀孤注一掷，终于捧起冠军奖杯，为校园电竞生涯交上完美的答卷。
迈入第五年，TCL 敢为不凡杯持续深耕高校电竞生态，不止是搭建竞技舞台，更致力于为青年学子提供展现热爱、磨砺意志的平台，以电竞传递青春拼搏、永不言弃的精神，让校园电竞成为大学生成长路上一段独特的经历。
集结 LPL 量级嘉宾倾力助阵：S10 亚军 Angel 向涛、西安 WE 队长 Monki 王梦齐、LPL 官方解说毛毛同台献声。兼具职业赛场洞察力与成熟解说功底的三位嘉宾，以硬核视角拆解战局，为现场与线上观众带来高规格的沉浸式观赛体验。
紧张的正赛之外，Angel、Monki、毛毛三位解说嘉宾也走上赛场，组队开启趣味娱乐对局。面对新生代高校选手，嘉宾队没能拿下胜利，却全程氛围拉满，尽兴享受电竞本身的乐趣，也让赛场多了一份松弛热闹的青春气息。
本届赛事，TCL 27C3A Pro 显示器首次登陆敢为不凡杯，成为赛事指定用机。依托万象分区技术，屏幕控光精准细腻，草丛、阴影等暗部场景细节清晰可辨；搭载 Tmoc 超级动态锐利技术，有效解决英雄联盟团战技能释放时画面拖影、粘连的问题，高速对局画面干净利落；同时支持超高刷新率双模切换，可灵活适配 MOBA、FPS 等不同品类游戏，为选手带来稳定、专业的竞技视觉支撑。
FFALCON 雷鸟、RayNeo、TGIF 拓际、雷蛇、维能、网鱼电竞为本届赛事生态合作伙伴，为赛事全程护航。品牌方不仅为参赛选手提供专业比赛外设，保障赛场稳定发挥，同时带来丰富奖品，助力高校电竞热爱落地。
不止有精彩的电竞对决，本次总决赛现场还搭建了 TCL 专属产品体验区，为到场的选手、观众和电竞爱好者带来丰富的科技体验。TCL Q10M Pro 极景 SQD-MiniLED 电视、冰箱、洗衣机、空调、32X3B 显示器悉数亮相，从画质出众的大屏影音设备、专业电竞显示器，到一站式智慧家电，多品类新品集中展出。大家可以自由上手体验，亲身感受前沿显示技术与智慧家居带来的体验升级，在热血赛事之外，解锁科技带来的别样乐趣。
TCL敢为不凡杯全球高校电子竞联赛早已不止是一场电竞赛事，更是品牌和青年对话、传递敢为不凡精神的舞台。品牌以赛场传递敢为不凡的精神，让硬件在实战中打磨，倡导团结、自律的正向竞技文化。TCL 将持续扩容赛事生态，愿做耐心的搭台人，以科技守护青年热爱，守护每一份赤诚，让每一份不甘平凡的努力，都拥有被看见的机会。

news.title: 文化“新三样”出海典型案例发布，完美世界《异环》入选
news.summary_raw: 2026中国文化"新三样"出海典型案例发布，完美世界自研游戏《异环》入选年度优秀网游出海典型案例，其全球公测后表现亮眼，海外流水贡献高于国内。

members.title: 文化“新三样”出海典型案例发布，完美世界《异环》入选

news.body:
2025年，中国网络文学海外市场营收达56.4亿元；中国自主研发游戏海外市场实际销售收入达204.55亿美元，同比增长10.23%；微短剧海外市场规模达36亿美元……
近年来，我国各种文艺形态蓬勃发展，为新大众文艺写下生动注脚。以网络文学、网络游戏、网络影视剧为代表的文化“新三样”，正在加速走向世界，成为中国文化出海的重要力量。
11月10日，作为第二十届杭州文博会重点产业对接活动——2026中国文化“新三样”出海典型案例观察暨产业对接合作会在国家（杭州）短视频基地余杭创作运营中心举办。大会现场发布《2026中国文化出海“新三样”优质内容风貌与产业发展》研究报告，完美世界自研游戏产品《异环》作为“中国文化‘新三样’出海年度优秀网游出海典型案例”入选，出海成果受行业认可。
完美世界集团高级副总裁、总编辑伊迪表示，游戏出海，精品内容是核心吸引力，成熟的出海体系则是触达全球用户的通路。完美世界坚持精品战略，推动优质数字内容走向海外市场，《异环》正是其中的典型代表。
今年4月末，《异环》开启全球公测，覆盖180多个国家和地区。公测以来，其在海内外主要区域多次进入iOS游戏畅销榜前五，并在日本等海外市场多次登顶PS主机热门榜。截至10月28日，《异环》全球累计流水超27亿元人民币，其中海外累计流水贡献已高于国内市场，收获海外玩家广泛认可。
《异环》在海外市场的亮眼成绩，离不开团队一次次对内容的精雕细琢，对于玩法的颠覆创新。作为一款超自然都市开放世界RPG，产品将游戏框架聚焦“都市模拟”。在这座城市中，玩家不仅可以与异象战斗，更可以开餐厅、送快递、组乐队等，有丰富的都市生活玩法可以自由选择。研发团队依托 UE5.6、DLSS4 等前沿技术，大幅优化场景的纹理细节和光影效果，增强游戏沉浸感；上线的云游戏版本《云·异环》移动端、PC端，既不会占用设备过多空间，还能让玩家在感受高品质的情况下，畅享游戏的乐趣。
在深耕研发的同时，完美世界还依托焕新升级的全球化发行体系为产品赋能。《异环》的国内市场及海外绝大部分区域均由公司自主发行。公司因地制宜对各地区采取差异化发行策略，结合产品特性、用户画像、不同国家及地区的市场环境等，以精细化、国际化、多元化的发行策略，助力游戏取得良好市场成绩。
不只《异环》，完美世界多年来始终立足全球，积极开拓海外市场，多款产品收获海外玩家广泛认可。比如，2025年6月末至7月初，异世界都市冒险JRPG游戏《女神异闻录：夜幕魅影》（《P5X》）相继在日本、欧美、东南亚等海外区域公测，公测首日即空降日本、欧美等多地iOS游戏免费榜榜首，并冲入日本iOS畅销榜TOP3，同时登顶Steam全球下载榜首位。更早之前，轻科幻开放世界游戏《幻塔》主机版本上线首日即进入日、韩、美、德、法等多个国家和地区的新游畅销榜前三，并在第二天迅速登顶，连续多日稳居新游畅销榜前五。在长年的出海实践中，完美世界不断沉淀出丰富的可复用出海经验，为产品出海打开空间。
未来，公司将继续深入推进精品化、多元化、国际化、技术赋能的发展战略：一方面持续深耕在营游戏，挖掘长线价值；另一方面稳步推进在研游戏并加强出海业务。与此同时，公司还将继续紧抓创新技术研发与前沿技术应用，以技术创新让内容创意落地生根，更好地服务于用户体验。

news.title: Bloody Hell Hotel Developer on Making a Vampire Management Sandbox
news.summary_raw: Wlad Marhulets, the former film composer behind DARQ, talked to us about the development of Bloody Hell Hotel, discussing the mechanics of its vampire hotel sandbox, how the procedural dungeons were designed, and why the studio works with contractors instead of full-time employees.

members.title: Bloody Hell Hotel Developer on Making a Vampire Management Sandbox

news.body:
Bloody Hell Hotel Developer on Making a Vampire Management Sandbox
Wlad Marhulets, the former film composer behind DARQ, talked to us about the development of Bloody Hell Hotel, discussing the mechanics of its vampire hotel sandbox, how the procedural dungeons were designed, and why the studio works with contractors instead of full-time employees.
Please introduce yourself to our readers. What projects have you contributed to before Bloody Hell Hotel?
Hey, my name is Wlad Marhulets, also known as Mr. Dev to the audience of Bloody Hell Hotel. I've worked on projects across a few different industries over the years. The game that started it all and paved the way for Bloody Hell Hotel was DARQ, which I developed almost solo, with virtually no budget. It went on to accumulate over 7 million downloads across PC and consoles (most of those came from a free Epic Games Store promotion – not direct sales).
Bloody Hell Hotel is a very different beast, though – it's an AA-scale production involving over 150 collaborators from around the world. But DARQ did sell a copy or two, so during the COVID lockdowns, I decided to write a book, "GAMEDEV: 10 Steps to Making Your First Game Successful" – given the cheesy title, I honestly didn't think many people would read it. To my surprise, it became an Amazon bestseller, and some schools even use it as part of their game design curriculum – still pinching myself.
Before getting into game development, I worked as a film composer. I was lucky enough to collaborate with Bob Shaye, the executive producer of The Lord of the Rings, and contribute additional music to films like The Giver, Hitman: Agent 47, The November Man, and Sabotage. And yet, one of the most widely heard pieces of music I've ever written was for a cat litter commercial. Really. It ran on TV for so many years that it serves as a much-needed reminder that my career as a film composer wasn't as glamorous as it might sound.
How did your background in film and music influence your approach to animation and audio?
A strong understanding of video editing, cinematography, lighting, color, and music transfers to video game development in unexpected ways. I don't think many studios approach audio the same way we do. We don't just cut a trailer and then look for good background music. Our trailers are essentially music videos – which might not be immediately obvious.
For Bloody Hell Hotel's announcement trailer, the music was written first, recorded with a live orchestra, and then used as the structural basis for the footage, which often had to be sped up and edited quite heavily to match the music. I don't think larger studios would be willing to take such a creative risk, but doing so landed us a Golden Joystick Award nomination for Best Trailer, alongside AAA titles.
Of course, taking creative risks can also produce unpredictable results. While our most recent trailer was praised for gameplay, the way we used the live choir was so experimental that the internet wiped the floor with us in the comments – and I think rightly so. We'll take it easy next time.
As for audio in general, needless to say, we pay enormous attention to it. For DARQ, all sound effects were created by Bjørn Jacobsen, known for his work on Cyberpunk 2077. He deserves all the credit for the sound awards DARQ has received. Bloody Hell Hotel also features extremely detailed sound effects. It's no longer the vision of a single sound designer, because the game is simply too big for that to be feasible. But our obsessive attention to detail in sound design has only increased since DARQ.
Similarly, musicality and rhythm carry over into animation. In Bloody Hell Hotel, we treat the movement of the player's hands almost like dance choreography. Whether you're interacting with an object, casting a spell, or smacking a guest in the face with a baguette, there's a surprising amount of choreography behind every gesture – as ridiculous as it sounds.
The goal is to make it all look effortless and spontaneous, much like a fight scene in a movie, where every gesture is deliberate, but the audience is never supposed to notice.
Please tell us about your unusual studio structure. Why did you decide to not hire full-time employees? How does it help develop Bloody Hell Hotel?
We've worked with over 150 contractors from all over the world on Bloody Hell Hotel so far. The main reason behind this structure? The game has so many interconnected systems that our development priorities naturally shift from one area to another. At times, we might be heavily focused on assets for the furniture system, which requires artists with a very different skill set than, for example, creating assets for procedurally generated dungeons, where the emphasis is on modular design and reusability. Some periods are animation-heavy, while others focus more on programming or VFX.
It doesn't always make sense to have all these specialists working full-time throughout development, even though we tend to collaborate with the same people over the years.
At any given time, we have about 15-30 contractors actively working on the game. The amount and variety of work that goes into Bloody Hell Hotel might suggest a much larger team, and in a way, that's accurate - just not everyone is working at the same time.
Many of our collaborators have been with us since the beginning, but their involvement naturally changes depending on what stage of development we're in or their own availability. This also gives us the luxury of not having to put unnecessary time pressure on our team members. There's no crunch time, because we can expand the team in any given department when needed. Instead of "Get this done by Thursday or we're screwed!" it's "So, when do you think you can get this done?" This allows us to plan ahead while keeping the team free from the pressure of internal deadlines.
Remote session with the VO actress, Madison Mitts, recording gibberish lines co-created with the BHH community
Different tasks also benefit from different approaches. Some call for the expertise of AAA veterans. Others benefit from someone equally talented who hasn't spent years working within established industry conventions, someone who's not afraid to experiment and run with bold ideas.
Of course, preserving a consistent creative vision in a structure like this requires extra effort. Detailed documentation helps a lot, but so does actually traveling to meet and work with key team members in person, often thousands of miles away from our studio's home base in Los Angeles.
Could you discuss the mechanics of the game? What makes it unique? What types of players will enjoy it?
OK, elevator pitch time! Bloody Hell Hotel is a first-person sandbox where you play as a vampire! Imagine waking up in your cozy coffin after centuries of captivity, discovering that your mansion is in ruins, and your vampiric powers are drained from... well, intermittent fasting spanning hundreds of years. What do you do? Turn your mansion into a hotel, obviously! Why? Because it's a lot easier to lure potential victims in and restore your vampiric powers than to run around hunting villagers like a goof. There's hotel management, farming, cooking, crafting, dungeon crawling, combat, and a whole bunch of other interconnected systems.
But here's the important part: almost everything is optional. You can run a perfectly peaceful hotel, spend your days farming and cooking, or close the hotel altogether and focus on forging weapons and exploring dungeons to become a ridiculously powerful vampire. You don't even have to kill anyone to survive – blood is separate from HP; it's needed to use vampiric powers, and you can simply buy blood from the Vampiric Council if you're one of those pacifist vampires. Or... you can unleash absolute mayhem in your hotel and feel ridiculously overpowered while delivering the last customer service experience your guests will ever have.
What excites me most is giving players the freedom to find their own ways of doing things. There are multiple ways to accomplish almost anything, and no single playstyle is the "correct" one. That's where most of the replayability comes from – well, there are also six vampiric classes with 270 skills in total, including upgrades, leveling up across five disciplines, countless perks, mutations, pets, upgrade trees for every major area in the game, and a variety of bat species to choose from.
Someone who loves cozy management games might have a completely different experience from someone who enjoys combat and exploration, even though they're playing the same game. And of course, if you enjoy a little bit of everything, you can do that too. But this isn't a game for everyone. There's combat, but it's not trying to be the next Dark Souls.
There's an in-game clock, but the gameplay is meant to be relaxing. Build a hotel, decorate it, furnish it, level up, unlock new skills, explore new areas, farm, cook, stare at the guests for too long and enjoy them expressing their discomfort in our custom-made gibberish language, and be ridiculous – that's the spirit of the game.
How did you set up procedural dungeon generation? What had you tried before settling on the final system? What worked and what didn’t?
We tried a lot of things that didn't work. It felt like inventing the lightbulb all over again – we got very good at discovering all the wrong ways to do it! We knew we wanted to generate a lot of content without giving players that "I've been here before" feeling. We also didn't want to rely on a minimap, which otherwise isn't needed in the game, just to keep players from getting disoriented. That made us realize that even a simple 90-degree corridor turn was a no-go. So, there are literally zero corridor turns in the dungeons.

news.title: End of Abyss Devs Explain How They Made Top-Down Horror Feel Unsettling
news.summary_raw: Former Little Nightmares developers discuss using practical-effects horror, anime framing, environmental lighting, and Metroidvania design to build their unsettling sci-fi adventure.

members.title: End of Abyss Devs Explain How They Made Top-Down Horror Feel Unsettling

news.body:
End of Abyss Devs Explain How They Made Top-Down Horror Feel Unsettling
Former Little Nightmares developers discuss using practical-effects horror, anime framing, environmental lighting, and Metroidvania design to build their unsettling sci-fi adventure.
End of Abyss places the responsive combat and interconnected exploration of an action Metroidvania inside an oppressive underground facility filled with abandoned machinery, brutalist structures, and distorted creatures. Released on October 1 for PC, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X|S, the game follows combat technician Cel as an investigation into unexplained disturbances becomes a descent through the facility’s forgotten depths.
The project was developed by Malmö-based Section 9 Interactive, a small studio established by former Tarsier Studios developers whose previous work included Little Nightmares. However, the team’s influences extend well beyond games. Its visual direction draws from the craftsmanship of 1980s and 1990s movies, comics, and anime, particularly the practical effects of The Thing and the framing and animation of Akira and Ghost in the Shell. Older The Legend of Zelda and Metroid games also informed the creatures’ strangely appealing silhouettes.
In the following interview, Marcus Ottvall, Co-Founder of Section 9 Interactive, explains how End of Abyss evolved from a responsive action prototype into a more atmospheric horror experience. The team also discusses designing fear from a top-down perspective, creating interconnected environments, iterating on enemy concepts inside Unreal Engine, and balancing clear combat spaces against the darkness and uncertainty necessary for horror.
End of Abyss combines the unsettling atmosphere of psychological horror with top-down action combat and Metroidvania exploration. What was the original creative vision for the project, and how did it evolve throughout development?
Marcus Ottvall, Co-Founder of Section 9 Interactive: We began work on End of Abyss based on an older prototype that had the basic movement and gameplay gadgets. We discussed what direction to take if we were to create a finished product based on it. As we started to create the moodboards and some isolated test environments with enemies, we decided to go with the atmospheric approach of a fictional underground facility where something had gone wrong.
Several members of Section 9 Interactive previously worked on Little Nightmares at Tarsier Studios. How did that experience influence your approach to End of Abyss, particularly its art direction, environmental storytelling, atmosphere, and creature design?
Marcus Ottvall: The art direction of the games we previously worked on has been super strong, so it has probably influenced the way we approach certain elements of creating a world for the game. We still find it interesting for example to create environments and creatures that show what the place is about without telling much beyond that. We like the idea of the player exploring a world where there is a mystery about how areas are connected and slowly getting hints of what the bigger picture is.
What were the biggest artistic inspirations behind this world, and how did you establish its visual language?
Marcus Ottvall: The inspiration for this game mostly comes from the things that we grew up with. We really like the movies, games, comic books and anime created around the 1980s and 1990s. The craftsmanship had to be particularly good back then and the more manual work gave it a special feel. Movies like The Thing, for example, used animatronics and practical effects and set pieces, and anime movies like Ghost in the Shell and Akira had incredible animation and framing of scenes.
We tried to rely on basic ways to show and maintain the impression of the world. For example, by starting the game showing large, empty shafts, along with creaking metal and chunky concrete structures, we wanted to establish the basic premise of the location that you are in. We then tried to create certain scenes and areas throughout the game that would have similar elements, to remind the player that they are in this large interconnected underground environment.
How did you approach lighting, camera framing, environmental composition, and visual storytelling to preserve a feeling of dread when players can see much of their surroundings? It's a very unique combination of art styles and perspectives.
Marcus Ottvall: To bring out the sense of horror we used some basic elements. Being underground meant we couldn’t create too much natural ambient light, so we had to create our own fictional ambience. We could also utilize the lack of natural light to keep parts of an environment dark by lighting the scenes with only one or a few light sources. We also used dust and fog particles to create a sense of atmosphere. In some areas, the flashlight helped a lot making them creepy to explore. It was a constant challenge to show enough of the environment for players to easily navigate and engage in combat, while trying to keep it creepy enough to maintain a sense of unease.
Beside that, we felt that much of the fear comes from not knowing what you are about to experience, so we tried to lean into that when we were able to, setting up scenarios that could surprise the player or keep them on edge.
Can you walk us through your environment art and level design process, from early blockouts and reference gathering to modeling, materials, lighting, and final implementation?
Marcus Ottvall: We collected a lot of references for the environments, some of which we were able to use as inspiration when creating the concept art. We knew that we wouldn’t be able to create concepts for every room in the entire game so for some areas, we had discussions based on references and went on to block them out from there. We would then apply the first art pass to the areas that we were most comfortable with, and iterate on others by modifying and recreating blockouts that we felt were lacking. We tried to complement this with paintover concepts and by mocking up extra environment areas.
It differed slightly for areas that contained combat/exploration and for areas that held more artistic or story set pieces but we mostly went with this approach.
How did the team approach creature creation, and what did the production pipeline look like from early concepts and animation prototypes to finished encounters?
Marcus Ottvall: Besides the inspirations mentioned before, we like the almost cute aesthetic of games like the older Legend of Zelda or Metroid games. When creating the characters, we started off by discussing an enemy’s features and attack patterns, and tried to develop a character that would fit those gameplay features while still feeling like a part of the world. We sketched a lot of quick concepts, implemented quick animations and feature mockups in the engine until we found something that we liked. From there we went back to trying to figure out a final concept and then creating the final model, rig and animations. In some cases we went through fewer iterations, in others we had to work through quite a lot of them to get closer to what we were looking for.
How did you approach designing Cel's movement, weapons, dodging, enemy reactions, and combat feedback while making sure the gameplay remained consistent with the game's atmosphere?
Marcus Ottvall: The rather responsive movement comes from the prototype version of the game, and that was something that we liked, so we kept the base of it but tuned it towards something that would fit the more atmospheric approach. We wanted to make weapons and bullets to feel like they had a solid impact on enemies and tried to implement reactions and simple destruction for the enemies to enhance that. We also wanted Cel to not feel too static in the world, while not allowing her to jump or run anywhere. So we approached that by creating specific animations for interactions and reactions, where she would interact with computer panels, fall to the ground from an explosion or a heavy impact, or get thrown by a large enemy.
What software, engine features, and production tools did the team use to build End of Abyss? Were there any particularly interesting technical solutions or custom workflows developed for its environments, enemy behaviors, animation, rendering, or lighting?
Marcus Ottvall: We used Unreal Engine 4, and then moved to UE5. For asset creation we used Maya, Blender, ZBrush, Substance Painter and Photoshop as our main software programs. We used some plugins for the different software and created simple enemy destruction and behavior systems, but we are not the most technical team, so we mostly used familiar game development tricks to achieve many of the visual and gameplay elements, including some that might look somewhat technical.
Looking back on that process, what were the biggest creative or technical challenges, and what lessons would you share with other smaller studios attempting to build a similarly ambitious 3D experience?
Marcus Ottvall: The Metroidvania aspect was particularly challenging because it took a lot of time to test and iterate on. Creating connected rooms that you need to be able to transition smoothly between through multiple entrances and exits was also tricky. Another problematic and common aspect of creating games was that we became so good at playing our game that it was hard to get a feel for the balance of gameplay difficulty.

members.title: 把圈外人都拉入坑的奥克兰玩家嘉年华，和腾讯这款天花板产品有关

news.body:
“过去两年很愉快，希望接下来还能再有二十年。”
如果选一个词来形容刚刚结束的ExileCon 2026，我会想到“大型桌游现场”。
今年是第三届ExileCon——这是由《流放之路》系列开发商Grinding Gear Games（后称GGG）举办的全球玩家嘉年华，融合游戏新内容发布、现场试玩、开发者交流和玩家社区活动于一身。
时隔3年，GGG再次举办ExileCon，其中一个很重要的原因是：《流放之路2》经过两年的Early Access（抢先体验），即将在12月推出免费的1.0正式版本，而由腾讯运营的国服《流放之路：降临》也将采用这套完整内容。而在这么大版本的更新下，宣告转免费更是一次有勇气的尝试——这也与游戏即服务（GaaS）的理念相符。国服《流放之路：降临》此前已通过降价、不定期折扣、1元体验活动等多种形式让更多玩家以更低的门槛体验到瓦尔克拉斯大陆的魅力，在26年底宣告转免便是水到渠成。
受腾讯《流放之路》国服邀请，我第一次来到ExileCon。现场玩家来自世界各地，大部分是专门从海外飞来参与活动的，甚至有相当多的中国玩家。很多没有能亲自来到现场的国服玩家，也通过同步直播转播体验了ExileCon的全过程，直播间在线观看人数直奔“999+”。只不过让我有点意外的是，现场最受玩家欢迎的活动是《奥杜尔符文》——这是GGG为ExileCon特供的现场限定小游戏。
包括我在内，每位来到ExileCon的玩家都会在入场时随机收到一组卡牌，卡牌对应《流放之路》系列中的基础装备。GGG 的员工则会在现场扮演怪物，他们穿着印有怪物名称和攻防属性的 T 恤。玩家可以打出对应要求的卡牌，战胜对方，获得随机掉落的新装备卡牌和制作材料——工作人员也会通过贴纸等方式，为卡牌增加属性、提升品质，随着装备不断完善，玩家便能挑战更强的怪物和首领，争取更好的奖励。
这套卡牌游戏的设计很有意思。《流放之路》是一款强调装备随机掉落和角色构筑的ARPG，卡牌玩法保留了游戏中的核心循环：打怪、获取装备、制作装备，再不断调整自己的Build。也因此，来到现场之后，我要做的不只是观看演讲、试玩游戏或购买周边，更像是真的进入了一个小型的瓦尔克拉斯大陆。
“轻松”、“亲切”，是ExileCon给人最直观的感受。这也和Jonathan对整个ExileCon的期待相同。在进入会场之初，每当我犹豫要不要试试卡牌对战的时候，不经意和扮演怪物的开发者对上眼神，他们立即会主动示意让我去挑战他们。我还看到一些开发者，不仅自己扮演怪物，自己也在寻找不同的同事参加对战。
在挑战原始鬼灵（Primal Spirit）时，我和它的扮演者、负责游戏引擎开发的Thomas聊了几句。Thomas告诉我，有一些人会主动去挑自己想扮演的怪物，有一些人是来到现场的当天，随机领到的角色。也因此，不只是玩家，他们的一些同事也是现场才学会的规则。
“几乎所有员工都来了。”另一位开发者和我说。他负责初代作品《流放之路》相关内容，而《流放之路》将在11月13日迎来赛季更新，忙碌的周末结束之后，他没办法休息，需要立马投入到新赛季更新内容的工作中。
“还有很多事情没有处理完。虽然有些累，但不管怎么说，这是一个很好地跟玩家以及同事见面的机会。”他告诉我，“并且因为平时我专注于《流放之路》的内容，没有时间了解《流放之路2》的进展，但我一直非常好奇他们在开发的新东西，所以也正好来了解一下情况。”
这位开发者提到的新内容，便是在今年的ExileCon主题演讲环节正式公布的新职业暗影（Shadow）。作为ExileCon最重要的环节，主题演讲也延续了Jonathan提到的“轻松、亲切”氛围。
通常来说，在如此关键的场合，为避免出错或者出糗，游戏公司会选择以播片的方式来展示新职业的玩法。但GGG选择让《流放之路2》游戏总监Mark Roberts现场操作。在Mark上台前，Jonathan还开玩笑说：“这次尽量不要死，好吧？”这句话引起了现场玩家的一片笑声。
“游戏策划一定要玩游戏”，是中文玩家社区流传甚广的一句话。Mark显然一直都在玩，而且他本身就是因为玩得够好，才加入的GGG。加入工作室之后，Mark一边工作，一边仍能在《流放之路》竞速赛（One Month Race）中保持前20名。
这次在现场，Mark为大家演示了将在1.0版本推出的新职业暗影。十几分钟的时间，他熟练地使用潜行、布置陷阱，切换不同的技能组合，向玩家展示了暗影的多种玩法，最后还成功击败了区域首领“阿曼多，堕落之猪”（Armando the Showman）。
只不过，演示中途出现了一个小插曲：Mark不小心被一只金色精英怪Gemling Lieutenant（古灵副官）的一记重击直接击倒。现场玩家立刻发出一阵哄笑。
更意外的是，Mark的这次暴毙还提前曝光了一项此前尚未公布的新功能——死亡回顾（Death Summary），在即将更新的1.0版本中，制作团队进行了包括死亡回放、性能优化在内大量底层体验功能的更新。从展示界面中，玩家可以看到角色死亡前受到的伤害及其构成。注意到这一新功能后，现场玩家的掌声变得更热烈，甚至有人吹起了口哨。
“现在正好借这个机会告诉大家，我们做了死亡回顾功能。”Jonathan顺势在台上救场说，“好了，让我们回到刚才被打断的演示中吧。”
演示过程中被重要展现的暗影、决斗者两个新增基础职业，和配套的全新升华分支，是这次演讲的重点之一。
暗影以匕首和陷阱为主要攻击手段，并为《流放之路2》带来了一套全新的潜行机制。进入潜行状态后，玩家可以避开一定范围外怪物的侦测，再选择目标，利用技能迅速接近敌人并发动伏击。部分技能在潜行状态下还会获得额外效果。这让暗影有了不同于传统近战职业的战斗方式。
每当Jonathan介绍到新职业的关键机制，现场玩家都会用掌声和欢呼回应。我印象最深的一次，发生在他介绍决斗者（Duelist）的时候。
决斗者并不是这次ExileCon才首次公开的职业，它此前已经在今年的Gamescom上亮相。这次演讲主要展示了它的两个新升华职业，其中一个是骑士（Knight）。骑士最特别的设计，是可以召唤一名侍从（Squire）。
当侍从出现在屏幕上时，现场玩家的反应各不相同：有人惊呼，有人鼓掌，也有人看到侍从的模样后忍不住笑了起来。因为它看起来确实有点像个刚入门的“菜鸟”。Jonathan在现场稍微平静后补充：“不过，一旦有人归你指挥，你的责任就是为他们配齐装备。”
玩家们立刻欢呼起来。和一般的召唤物不同，骑士的侍从可以由玩家直接配置装备和技能宝石。它使用什么武器、掌握哪些技能，都由玩家决定。换句话说，玩家不仅要考虑自己的角色构筑，还要为侍从安排一套独立的装备和技能组合。这也为《流放之路：降临》的召唤物玩法增加了新的构筑空间。
除了新增职业外，Jonathan也介绍了即将到来的1.0版本更新的全貌。在历经两年抢先体验阶段后，这次版本的更新体量堪称海量：补全第五、六章主线剧情，推出系列规模最大的单人章节；上线全新赛季玩法“瓦尔克拉斯征服者”，加入攻城、阵营争夺、领地征伐的大规模对抗机制；同时追加数百款全新装备、天赋节点、传奇基底，重做大量BD体系。
在演讲现场，Jonathan花了近两个小时才介绍完这些内容——现在，你已经能立刻在社交平台刷到国服主播们对这些内容的总结和补充；而且，这些内容全部都将随1.0版本永久免费向所有玩家开放，这让这次更新在刷宝ARPG赛道里显得格外有分量。
在我看来，在刷宝ARPG大多以小步迭代的赛季为核心节奏的行业环境下，《流放之路2》这种一次性交付的超量完整内容，在传统刷宝、构筑配装的核心框架之上，塞入了完整长线叙事、大规模阵营攻防、全新职业体系等大量跨维度内容，无疑拓展了刷宝品类的空间，对整个赛道来说也是一次标志性的尝试。
随《流放之路2》正式1.0接下来的上线，GGG将进入同时运营两款大型ARPG的新阶段。可以预见，上线后，“流放之路”系列的玩家规模还将迎来新一轮增长。在媒体群访中，我不由有些好奇：GGG将如何应对同时开发和运营两款游戏带来的挑战？
Jonathan告诉我，过去几年里，GGG为了实现两款游戏的同步开发，对工作室的组织架构进行了多次调整。如今，两个项目已经基本分成了相对独立的团队：《流放之路》的具体开发工作主要由Octavian和Andrew负责，而Jonathan和Mark则将更多精力放在《流放之路2》上。
“当然，我依然会参与各种方案的讨论，但现在更多是以顾问的身份提供建议。真正负责执行和推进《流放之路》开发工作的是他们。”Jonathan说，“让整个工作室具备同时开发两款游戏的能力，过去确实是一件非常困难的事情。不过现在我们终于能够做到。”
在整个介绍和交流的过程中，我也能感受到他对各个地区玩家的重视——比如，在提问环节，Jonathan在一些问题中会特意提到“中国玩家也非常关心这一点”。
GGG目前一共有265名员工。这对一家位于新西兰的游戏工作室来说，并不容易。新西兰远离欧美等传统游戏开发中心，本地人才储备相对有限，游戏开发又是一个高度依赖人才的行业。何况，他们需要面对非常多来自不同地区、拥有不同文化的玩家群体，尤其还有广阔的中国玩家。
Jonathan向我们透露说，他坚持亲自面试每一位员工。在他看来，面对面的交流非常重要，他喜欢直接和员工沟通。“我们工作室基本不开正式会议。需要沟通时，我会直接去找相关同事，或者让他们来找我。”Jonathan说，“对我而言，最不能放弃的，就是和员工、和玩家面对面交流。”
从这个角度看，无论ExileCon现场卡牌游戏让玩家和开发者面对面的设计，还是主题演讲时，游戏总监亲自上场为玩家演示游戏玩法内容，GGG与玩家的沟通方式，似乎都是Jonathan在这一理念上的延续。而在下周二，他还将亲自来到上海，和国服玩家面对面。
而在国区专访环节，一位《流放之路：降临》主播提到，在0.5和0.5.5版本期间，他在中国社区组织了两轮专家独狼自力赛季。他想要知道，GGG今后是否会为这类比赛提供更多支持，比如私人赛季、可调整的规则或词缀，他也希望中国玩家未来在赛事方面获得GGG的支持。
“当然，我确实希望多做一些这方面的事情。”Jonathan爽快地回答，“二代目前还没有太多时间来做这些，不过大家肯定有兴趣。我非常愿意推进这件事，也想在私人赛季方面做得更多，我认为会很有意思。”
活动最后一天下午，创始人圆桌结束后，Chris Wilson和Jonathan一起出现在见面会的签名桌前。Chris Wilson是GGG的联合创始人，也是初代《流放之路》的灵魂制作人，他在2023年底卸任了公司的管理职务，在2024年短暂宣布退休之后，他又在2025年创立了新的工作室，准备开发一款规模“比《流放之路》小得多”的游戏。
其实，前一天我就看到Chris站在会场的一个角落里，想找他合影、交流的玩家在一旁排起了长队。想想这两天的ExileCon，我始终觉得这里有一种难得的纯粹。即使已经离开GGG，Chris依然会回到ExileCon来，也依然受到玩家的尊重和喜爱——无论你是游戏公司的创始人、开发者，还是远道而来的玩家，当你来到ExileCon，又都成为了瓦尔克拉斯大陆的一部分。
举办这次的ExileCon的场地奥蒂亚中心一共能容纳2000多人，活动门票很早就售罄了。在第一届ExileCon举办时，Chris曾透露过，当时《流放之路》的玩家只有不到1%是新西兰本地玩家，而当年参加ExileCon的人里，有超过90%来自海外，许多中国玩家甚至是远渡重洋奔赴南半球。是什么吸引这么多人，愿意为了一款游戏的线下活动飞超过10小时的路程？
我们或许可以从其他地方知晓答案——今年5月，新版本“远古回响”推出后，《流放之路：降临》在国内B站、NGA等玩家平台收获了大量好评，1.0版本的转免预约也是国服玩家之间持续热门的话题。这证明了在持续更新的过程中，它始终能够持续吸引大量玩家回到游戏，也验证了GGG一直以来的思路：不靠付费锁内容，而是把一整套打磨完成的庞大玩法、故事交给玩家。
那些没有能实际前来，选择在线上观看活动的国内外玩家，也纷纷在直播评论里留下相当热情的文字。其中点赞最高的一条是：“没有哪家公司能像 GGG 这样。能够成为他们的玩家，本身就是一种荣幸。谢谢你们！”
而在下周二，《流放之路：降临》国服1.0前瞻试玩会将在上海举办，Jonathan也会来到现场，和国服玩家面对面交流。届时，国服玩家也能试玩到ExileCon揭晓的全新职业。
虽然，就和所有的持续运营游戏一样，或许对于GGG和腾讯国服来说，当1.0版本正式上线时，挑战才真正开始。但就像有玩家说的那样：“过去两年很愉快，希望接下来还能再有二十年。”对他们来说，期待早在更早之前就开始产生了。

members.title: Bandai Namco closes Reflector Entertainment, expects to post €21m loss in Q3 as a result

news.body:
Bandai Namco closes Reflector Entertainment, expects to post €21m loss in Q3 as a result
Unknown 9 developer was acquired by Bandai Namco in 2020
Bandai Namco is closing Unknown 9: Awakening developer Reflector Entertainment.
In a press briefing, Bandai Namco stated that "after comprehensively considering future business plans, necessary additional investment, and the possibility of profitability and business continuation," it has decided to dissolve and liquidate Reflector.
The publisher expects to "post an extraordinary loss of approximately €21 million" for Reflector in its Q3 financial results for the fiscal year ending March 31, 2027.
Bandai Namco acquired Montreal-based Reflector in 2020 for an undisclosed sum. It also acquired the studio's subsidiary, Reflector Interactive Productions.
Reflector was founded in 2016 by Alexandre Amancio and Lune Rouge.
Reflector is known for the 2024 action-adventure title Unknown 9: Awakening. It was created as a transmedia franchise, including a podcast audio drama, novels, and a comic book series.
A month after launch, the studio announced it had cut 18% of its workforce.
The studio attributed the layoffs to a new development phase, stating that affected employees weren't assigned to roles its active projects needed at the time.
Further redundancies occurred in 2025 after the decision "not to greenlight" an unannounced project. The studio also cancelled the Unknown 9 franchise due to low sales.
Reflector CEO Hervé Hoerdt acknowledged that Unknown 9 did not meet expectations "despite numerous timeline adjustments and investments."
"This decision correlates directly with the failure of the studio's ambitious and courageous first project, a new IP with a rich transmedia universe."

members.title: Skydance announces layoffs to games division following $111bn merger

news.body:
Skydance announces layoffs to games division following $111bn merger
"We have taken some time to consider where we are investing our efforts and have made the difficult decision to scale down some of our projects"
Skydance has implemented an undisclosed number of cuts to its games division.
A spokesperson told Variety the company is "implementing reorganisation and operational shifts across a few areas of [its] business" following last month's $111 billion merger between Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery.
"We have stepped back and taken some time to consider where we are investing our efforts and have made the difficult decision to scale down some of our projects. As a result, there are roles impacted."
The spokesperson continued: "This is not a reflection of the talent, dedication, or creativity of those affected, and we are grateful for their contributions. We are committed to approaching the process with transparency, care, and respect for those who are leaving the company."
According to Kotaku and Insider Gaming, approximately 30 positions may be affected. This includes associate design director David Ballard, who announced his departure on LinkedIn.
"My chapter with Skydance and Paramount came to an end today with a layoff," wrote Ballard. "I'm super grateful for the opportunities I was given over the past almost 4.5 years. A shipped title, several awards, two promotions, an incredible team, and an unbelievable amount of creativity and collaboration."
Skydance CEO David Ellison previously stated that the merger would require the company to make "difficult decisions."
"Bringing together two companies of this size and complexity will require difficult decisions. There will be changes, and there will be impacts. I'm not going to pretend otherwise."
Paramount Games Studio was established this summer and is led by EVP and head of games Dan Brigg. The studio has combined Paramount's IP with Skydance Interactive and Skydance New Media.
Following the acquisition, it merged with WB Games to form a single unit led by Tony Driscoll.

members.title: Agent自演进驶入“双轨时代”！openJiuwen首发TTSE经验学习框架

ai.body:
Agent自演进驶入“双轨时代”！openJiuwen首发TTSE经验学习框架
让每一次任务，都成为下一次进步的起点
允中 发自 凹非寺
量子位 | 公众号QbitAI
Agent越用越强，为什么还会被环境“绊倒”？
你的同事用Agent整理报表，一路顺畅。你用同样的模型、工具和流程，换成自己的文件，却开始反复试读、频繁返工。
模型没变，Harness没变，换个环境，为什么就不灵了？
文件位置不同、数据格式混杂、模板约束变化，都可能让原本有效的方法失效。模型提供推理能力，Harness组织执行流程，但Agent仍需判断：这里的环境是什么样的，过去的经验还适不适用？
这也揭示了Agent持续自我改进过程中一个容易被忽视的问题：Agent不仅要从任务中学会“怎么做”，还要判断这些经验在什么环境下仍然有效。
在RSI（Recursive Self-Improvement，递归自我改进）的持续优化过程中，Agent可以通过任务反馈改进执行方法、积累可复用经验。但如果环境认知没有同步更新，过去有效的经验也可能成为新的障碍：接口条件变了，还在重试旧调用；数据格式变了，还在沿用旧规则。
一次失败，究竟该改方法，还是该纠正对环境的认识？
Agent的新难题，藏着认知科学的老线索
认知科学对知识结构的研究，为区分这两类问题提供了启发：
1983年，认知科学家John R. Anderson在ACT-R相关理论研究中，系统讨论了人类知识中的两类重要形式：
- 陈述性知识（Declarative Knowledge）：描述“世界是什么样的”。例如，关闭的容器会遮挡内部物体，打开后才能观察。
- 程序性知识（Procedural Knowledge）：描述“应该如何行动”。例如，需要寻找多个同类物体时，找到第一个之后，还应继续检查其他可能的位置。
将这一视角引入Agent，就能看到：认识环境与掌握做法，彼此关联，却需要不同的验证与更新方式。环境判断要核对是否符合现场事实，行动方法要检验在相应条件下是否有效。混淆两者，就可能把偶然成功的操作当成稳定规律，或在环境变化后继续沿用失效的方法。
沿着这一思路，openJiuwen在RSI方向的持续探索中，进一步提出TTSE（Two-Track Self-Evolution，双轨自演进）。
在此前发布的双维度RSI框架介绍中，openJiuwen已通过Harness+Artifacts双维度优化，让Agent能够基于真实任务反馈，持续改进工作方法与交付成果。而TTSE则进一步聚焦经验本身的可靠性与可复用性，不仅让Agent积累有效的执行方法，还要持续校正对环境的认识，避免经验在环境变化后失效。
为此，TTSE借鉴认知科学中对陈述性知识与程序性知识的区分，将任务中获得的经验分为两条轨道：
- FACT（环境事实）：持续核对和更新“这个环境是什么样的”。
- TIP（条件式技巧）：持续改进“在这些条件下应该怎么做”。
TTSE双轨框架：构建反馈驱动的经验自演进闭环
分清经验的类型，只是第一步。如何让Agent从任务反馈中持续学习，并将有效经验转化为下一轮执行的改进？
这也是RSI的核心思路：通过真实任务反馈驱动改进，并在后续执行中不断验证和优化。TTSE将这一思路落实到经验管理层面，通过分批执行任务，让已有经验持续接受新证据的检验，判断哪些经验值得保留、哪些需要修正或退役，再将更新后的经验用于下一轮任务。
框架由双轨知识表示、冷启动、在线增量演进、最终输出与评估四个部分组成，如下图所示：
① 双轨知识表示：让环境事实与执行方法各有依据
FACT用于描述环境本身的属性与规律，强调可直接验证，以及在适用场景下的跨任务稳定性；TIP用于描述特定任务条件下的执行方法，采用“在什么条件下，执行什么操作”的形式表达。
两类知识分别维护独立编号、呈现方式与证据追踪机制。这使每条经验都能被单独引用、核对和更新，也便于在执行出现问题时，追溯具体是哪条事实判断或操作建议产生了影响。
分类时，框架结合经验所描述的主体与作用进行判断（展开如何进行分类根据mechanism）；难以确定的内容默认归入TIP，降低将未经充分验证的操作经验误当成环境事实的风险。
② 冷启动：从首批任务中归纳初始经验
TTSE从空规则库出发，由Agent执行首批任务（chunk 0），再根据执行轨迹分别归纳FACT与TIP，建立初始双轨经验库。
这一阶段以归纳为主。由于尚无历史规则参与执行，因此不进行旧规则的归责与退役，而是为后续演进建立第一批有任务证据支撑的经验。
③ 在线增量演进：在新任务中检验并修正已有经验
后续任务按批次推进。每一轮，Agent加载上一轮的FACT与TIP，利用已有经验执行当前批次任务，再根据执行轨迹和评估结果，依次完成四个环节：
- 归因（Blame）：分析失败轨迹，识别可能误导执行的规则，为经验修正定位对象。
- 退役（Retire）：将被归责的规则移入退役池，并保留原因、批次和时间等记录，使调整过程可追溯。
- 矛盾分析与合成（Contradict / Synthesize）：检查退役规则中的矛盾，尝试识别其中隐含的适用条件，将看似冲突的经验合成为条件更明确的TIP。
- 归纳（Induce）：对比成功与失败轨迹，或从成功轨迹中提炼有效经验，通过新增、修订、确认与移除等操作，更新双轨经验库。
Blame→Retire→Contradict/Synthesize→Induce在多个任务批次间循环运行，使经验持续接受新证据的检验：既更新对环境的认识，也调整相应条件下的执行方法。
④ 最终输出与评估：检验经验演进带来的实际收益
经过多轮增量演进，框架输出最终的FACT与TIP经验库，并在测试任务中评估其对准确率或任务表现的影响。
这套机制的核心，是让环境事实与执行方法分别沉淀、各自可追溯，并在持续执行中得到检验与修正。Agent每完成一批任务，都能将新的交互证据转化为下一轮可使用的经验，逐步形成从环境交互到知识更新、再到行动改进的闭环。
“但一个关键问题仍待回答：将环境事实与行动技巧分开演进，是否真的比传统的单轨经验管理更有效？”
从机制到实证：五大基准，验证TTSE双轨自演进的有效性
TTSE的方法论与实验结果已在论文A Two-Track Online Self-Evolution Framework for LLM Agents中展开研究。
为了验证双轨经验机制是否真正有效，研究团队在ALFWorld、ScienceWorld、GDPevo、SOPBench和PinchBench五个基准上进行了评测，每项实验均进行三次独立重复，以考察方法的实际收益与运行稳定性。
五大基准，呈现多维度增益
- ALFWorld：成功率最高达到98.51%。在GLM-5上，TTSE成功率达到98.51%；在DeepSeek-V3.2上，成功率达到97.8%，较此前最优方法GraSP的83.6% 提升14.2个百分点，同时减少任务执行步数。
- ScienceWorld：任务表现显著提升。MACRO Reward从0.7204提升至0.8534，Native Success从53.08%提升至73.46%，提高20.38个百分点。
- GDPevo：双轨优于单轨。完整FACT+TIP方案的平均得分达到0.2616，约为零样本基线0.0947的2.8倍。仅使用TIP或FACT均未达到完整双轨方案的表现，验证了环境事实与行动技巧协同管理的价值。
- SOPBench：与贝叶斯技能管理融合后进一步提升。总体成功率从基线的79.15% 提升至单轨方案的91.59%，并进一步达到双轨融合方案的94.58%，较单轨方案额外提升2.99个百分点。
- PinchBench：真实世界任务中保持稳定增益。以非侵入方式将TTSE接入OpenClaw，在147个真实端到端任务上进行三次独立运行。双轨方案平均得分从0.7439提升至0.7822，增加3.83个百分点；三次运行的增益方向一致，运行极差也从3.33个百分点降至1.61个百分点。
这些结果覆盖具身交互、科学推理、企业运营、工业流程及真实世界端到端任务，表明TTSE的价值并不局限于某个特定模型或单一场景。
消融实验进一步回答：为什么必须双轨？
GDPevo的消融实验提供了更直接的证据：完整双轨方案优于只记录事实或只记录技巧的单轨方案。
原因在于，环境认知与行动策略承担着不同的职责。只有FACT，智能体可能知道环境的约束，却缺少合适的行动方法；只有TIP，智能体可能掌握操作技巧，却无法准确识别这些技巧成立的条件。只有将两者结合，才能同时回答「环境是什么样」和「在当前条件下应该怎么做」。
因此，双轨设计并非简单地将经验库拆成两部分，而是让不同类型的知识，按照各自的语义和适用条件进行归纳、验证与复用。
从跨模型、跨任务到真实世界评测，实验结果不仅验证了TTSE双轨经验机制的有效性，也进一步展示了RSI在经验学习层面的应用潜力：Agent可以在不改变模型参数的情况下，通过持续积累、验证与更新任务经验，逐步改善后续任务表现。
这也为TTSE从研究框架走向实际办公智能体产品提供了实证依据。
TTSE双轨自演进落地WorkSwarm
TTSE不仅在论文实验中验证了有效性，也已正式落地openJiuwen的WorkSwarm蜂群办公智能体。
想亲自体验TTSE？只需安装并启动WorkSwarm 0.2.7及以上版本，在设置中开启TTSE自演进开关，即可体验经验积累与复用带来的效率提升。
接下来，通过两个真实办公任务，一起来看看TTSE如何让Agent在实际执行中变得更快、更高效。
TTSE走进真实办公场景，让经验成为效率
在日常办公中，Agent已广泛应用于数据清洗与分析、文档编辑与整理、报表生成、信息提取及格式转换等任务。然而，面对不同的文件结构、数据格式和业务要求，Agent往往需要反复探索环境、尝试工具调用，并重新摸索任务的执行路径。
为了直观展示TTSE的实际效果，团队选取了Excel数据清洗和文档与表格整理两个典型办公场景，对比Agent在首次执行与注入经验后的表现。
从结果可以看到，两个场景均取得了不同程度的效率提升：
这些提升并非来自模型能力的变化，而是在所展示的对比任务中，Agent能够利用历史执行经验，更快识别环境约束并选择合适的处理方式。
那么，TTSE究竟沉淀了哪些经验，又是如何帮助Agent减少试错的？
案例一：Excel数据清洗——减少数据识别与处理试错
这类任务的难点不只是清洗数据，还包括定位输入文件、识别隐藏的数据格式问题，以及确定符合业务要求的去重规则。
首次执行时，Agent没有可复用的任务经验，需要自行探索输入文件位置、判断数据格式，并推导重复记录的处理规则。整个过程共发生57次工具调用，其中3次失败；总耗时6分22秒。
任务结束后，TTSE从真实执行轨迹中提炼出可复用的任务经验。它们不再只是对过去操作的记录，而是能够直接影响下一次执行的决策依据：
- 快速定位输入素材。当用户没有明确说明文件位置时，优先检查workspace/input，直接寻找上游文件，避免在无关的任务目录中反复探索，也省去不必要的用户追问。
- 深入识别数据问题。面对Excel中看似正常的日期、金额和文本，直接使用openpyxl检查原始存储值，识别文本型日期、货币符号、尾随空格等隐蔽问题，减少因读取方式不当导致的遗漏。
- 复用经过验证的去重规则。按业务字段进行分组，保留最早日期记录，并记录删除数量，不再从头推导去重口径，减少重复判断与试错。
再次执行相似任务时，这些经验直接参与工具选择与处理决策。工具调用降至20次，失败调用降至1次，总耗时缩短至1分48秒。
案例二：文档与表格整理——减少文件探索与格式试错
与Excel数据清洗不同，这类任务的主要难点在于文件位置未知、CSV编码与分隔符不明确，以及Word模板结构复杂。首次执行时，Agent需要逐步探索文件、识别格式，并确定合适的模板处理方式。
在文档与表格整理任务中，Agent首次执行耗时1分49秒，共调用工具27次，发生2次工具调用失败。任务完成后，TTSE从真实执行轨迹中沉淀出一组环境事实与操作技巧。
再次执行时，Agent不再从零开始探索文件目录、试探CSV的读取方式，也不必等到文档生成后才发现模板替换问题。它能够直接复用已验证的环境经验，提前选择更合适的工具和处理路径。
第二次执行耗时缩短至1分26秒，工具调用降至18次，失败次数降至1次。整体耗时缩短约21.1%，工具调用减少33.3%，失败调用减少50%。
相比简单地记住过去执行过哪些操作，TTSE更进一步，让Agent同时积累对环境的认识，以及在特定条件下有效的执行方法。
从经验积累到能力提升，关键在于正确复用。
两个办公案例展示了TTSE在实际任务中的应用价值：Agent不必每次都从零探索，而是能够将历史任务中验证有效的经验，转化为后续执行的参考依据。
这正是RSI希望实现的持续改进方式：让每一次任务执行不仅产生交付成果，也有机会为下一次执行积累有效经验。TTSE则通过FACT与TIP的双轨机制，让这种经验积累更加可验证、可更新和可复用。
然而，这些收益是否只存在于特定任务中，还是能够在更广泛的办公任务中得到体现？
TTSE在办公基准中展现综合收益
为了进一步评估TTSE在综合办公场景中的表现，团队在业界开源榜单WorkBuddy Office Bench上对WorkSwarm接入TTSE的效果进行了测试。
其不仅在任务表现上有所提升，同时也有效降低了Token消耗与工具调用开销：评测结果显示，相较原生效果，任务表现提升3.81%，并且在输入Token消耗上降低1.70%，在输出Token消耗上降低30.09%，平均工具调用次数减少2次。
写在最后
我们正处在Agent从「一次性工具」走向「持续进化伙伴」的拐点。
RSI的核心价值，不只是让Agent完成更多任务，而是让它能够从每一次真实执行中获得反馈、积累经验，并将这些经验转化为持续改进的能力。
从Harness与Artifacts的双维度优化，到TTSE对环境事实与执行技巧的双轨演进，openJiuwen正在探索让智能体持续自我改进的不同路径：既能优化工作方法与交付成果，也能不断校正环境认知、沉淀可靠经验。
TTSE为其中的经验自演进提供了一种可验证、可追溯的实现机制，这让Agent不仅学会“怎么做”，还能理解“在什么环境下这样做才有效”，并在一次次任务执行中不断完善自身。
经验不该是过眼云烟。让Agent既学会「怎么做」，更学会「世界是什么样」，这是它走向长期自主的第一课。

members.title: BotPsy: On-Device Personal Assistant with a Sub-Billion-Parameter Agentic Language Model

ai.body:
BotPsy: On-Device Personal Assistant with a Sub-Billion-Parameter Agentic Language Model
Frontier cloud LLMs carry high operational costs that can fluctuate unexpectedly, and relying on such third-party models introduces vulnerabilities, as providers can modify, deny, or deprecate access at any time. Furthermore, proprietary models offer limited customization for specific workflows, while posing risks to privacy, data control, and transparency. Besides, not every task demands frontier-level intelligence: small, specialized agents can be equally capable on specific tasks and significantly cheaper to run, since many routine or smaller workloads can be processed efficiently on-device. As intelligence per parameter continues to improve rapidly, we aim to stand at the forefront of this shift toward performant, privacy-focused, self-hosted models.
Tether AI Research introduces BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model introduce BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model designed for function calling and agentic workflows, built on top of Qwen3.5-0.8B and suitable for on-device deployment. BotPsy is a "personal assistant" that uses tools to perform a variety of simple tasks for the user, in domains such as web search & research, travel & lifestyle, commerce & finance, business & customer operations, device & vehicle control, files & documents, calendar, and email & messaging. Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty. BotPsy achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) tool-use and agentic performance for its size, outperforming every model of up to 1.2B parameters that we tested (Figures 1 and 2). Designed for secure on-device workflows, it provides exceptional instruction-following reliability and efficiency while keeping user data private. As a small model, BotPsy still makes mistakes and is not intended for high-stakes use; please read the Intended Use and Limitations for more information.
🤗 Model (safetensors) | 📦 GGUFs (bf16, Q8, Q4)
Copyright Complaints
We will take appropriate actions in response to notice of copyright infringement. If you believe your work has been used or copied in a manner that infringes upon your intellectual property rights, please email data-apps@tether.io identifying and describing both the copyrighted work and alleged infringing content to file a notice of infringement.
Key Highlights
Benchmark results
- Twice the performance of its base model: BotPsy roughly doubles the agentic capability of Qwen3.5-0.8B-Think on key benchmarks: BFCL v4 rises from 23.4 to 44.0, ACEBench from 30.1 to 58.7, and τ-bench from 23.2 to 51.5 (mean of the retail, telecom and banking subsets).
- Best agent in its category: BotPsy outperforms leading models in the ≤1.2B-parameter weight class (Qwen3.5-0.8B-Think, LFM2.5-1.2B-Think, MiniCPM5-1B-Think) on all six tool-use and agentic benchmarks: BFCL v4, ACEBench, τ-bench, ToolSandbox, Claw-Eval and BrowseComp-Plus.
- Outperforms its larger sibling: BotPsy has the highest score of all models tested on five of the six benchmarks, beating Qwen3.5-2B-Think, a model 2.5× its size, on BFCL v4 (44.0 vs 37.7), ACEBench (58.7 vs 55.4), τ-bench (51.5 vs 46.5), ToolSandbox (64.6 vs 41.2) and BrowseComp-Plus (4.5 vs 2.8). Only on Claw-Eval does Qwen3.5-2B-Think lead (48.9 vs 46.5).
Model capabilities
- More reliable in multi-turn workflows: On τ²-bench, where the agent must hold a long customer conversation, follow a strict policy, and act on the customer's behalf, it scores 82.5 in telecom, ahead of Qwen3.5-2B-Think (69.3). On BFCL v4's multi-turn tasks, it rises from 7.5 to 46.1 over its base, nearly double Qwen3.5-2B-Think (23.8). Grouped by application, its multi-step scores lead all models tested in commerce and services (58.3 vs 47.4 for the next best, Qwen3.5-2B-Think) and in device and system management (46.1 vs 31.9).
- Knows when (not) to call tools: An agent that acts must also know when not to act. On BFCL v4's hallucination tests, which check that the model declines when no appropriate tool exists, BotPsy scores 86.1, the highest of all models tested. On ACEBench's special cases, where the request is incomplete, contains wrong parameters, or cannot be served by the given tools, it scores 51.3, up from 13.7 for its base model.
- Follows instructions while preserving knowledge: BotPsy specializes in tool use while preserving general skills. Instruction following improves sharply, with IFEval rising from 59.7 to 90.8 and IFBench from 22.0 to 55.9, the highest IFBench score of all models tested. General knowledge also improves, with GPQA Diamond rising from 33.2 to 38.1 and MMLU-Pro from 41.6 to 48.9. On all four benchmarks, BotPsy outperforms every other model of 1.2B parameters or fewer that we tested.
Safety, efficiency and deployment
- Safer than leading models in its category: In automated red-teaming across six harm categories, BotPsy produces unsafe responses 21% of the time, compared with 36% for its base model. This is the lowest rate of all models of up to 1.2B parameters (LFM2.5-1.2B-Think: 35%; MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 47%). Under prompt-injection attacks, which matter most for agents that read untrusted tool outputs, the unsafe rate drops from 46% for its base model to 31%.
- More efficient reasoning and less looping: On questions that all five models answer correctly, BotPsy reaches the answer with about 3× fewer reasoning tokens than its base model on GPQA Diamond (3,690 vs 11,563) and 2.7× fewer on MMLU-Pro (1,912 vs 5,105). Across all IFBench attempts, its rate of getting stuck in repetitive reasoning loops falls from 22.9% to 1.4%, and runs that hit the 32k-token limit fall from 28.3% to 0.2%. Shorter, more decisive reasoning should reduce latency on-device.
- Open-source and ready to use: BotPsy will be released with open weights under the Apache 2.0 license for research and educational use. It will be available in three precisions (bf16, Q8, Q4), as Hugging Face safetensors and as GGUF files for the QVAC SDK and llama.cpp.
Broader Vision
Building upon the foundation of BotPsy, future development by Tether Data, S.A. de C.V. (“Tether AI Research”, “we”, “our”) will focus on expanding on-device agentic capabilities to seamlessly integrate with an even broader array of hardware and local services. Tether's Hypersearch will evolve to support more robust decentralized peer-to-peer (P2P) queries, further ensuring private, encrypted web searches that bypass corporate trackers. QVAC Fabric local fine-tuning mechanisms will be optimized to adapt more deeply to individual user preferences, workflows, and specialized tool environments. Future iterations will allow the smartphone interface to smoothly delegate heavy computational tasks to home PCs or trusted secure P2P nodes during offline-online transitions. Privacy protocols will be continuously strengthened to guarantee that all personal data, credentials, and decisions remain strictly on local hardware. Collaborative features will be introduced to allow secure agent-to-agent communication across trusted local networks without compromising user confidentiality. Ultimately, these advancements will solidify BotPsy as a fully autonomous, highly capable personal AI ecosystem that keeps users entirely in control of their digital lives.
Methodology
BotPsy is based on Qwen3.5-0.8B and is post-trained in four sequential stages: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Multi-teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD), and two rounds of Reinforcement Learning (RL). Each stage uses the previous stage's best checkpoint as its starting point and benefits from a different learning signal: imitation of reference trajectories, the token distributions of much larger teacher models, and rule-based tool-calling rewards (see Figure 3).
Training procedure: four stages, three types of feedback
Our approach uses four stages of training, which learn from three types of signal: demonstrations, specialist teachers, and verifiable rewards.
Learning from demonstrations (SFT)
We first perform full-parameter supervised fine-tuning on tool-use conversations. These include multi-turn agent trajectories from simulated environments, replayed single, parallel and multi-step calls, and cases where no tool should be called.
Learning from teachers (MOPD)
Next, the student is trained with on-policy distillation (OPD): it generates its own responses, and a specialist teacher provides feedback on every token, using the per-token reverse KL divergence as the training signal. To build the teachers, we first RL-trained three Qwen3.5-4B models to specialize in tool use, general reasoning, and instruction following. During training, every prompt is routed to one of these teachers. This stage mainly aims to recover knowledge and instruction following, which degraded during the SFT stage, although the tool-use metrics also increase (see Figure 4).
Learning from rules and environments (RL stages)
Finally, the model is trained with reinforcement learning using DAPO [1], learning only from rewards computed by rules and verifiers. The first round focuses on tool calling, accompanied by instruction following and STEM multiple-choice questions. As in Tool-N1 [2], the tool-calling reward first checks the reasoning and tool-call format. Instead of Tool-N1's binary correctness reward, however, it gives fine-grained partial credit in the spirit of ToolRL [3], matching the predicted tool names, argument names, and argument values against the ground truth.
The second round widens the training mix to general-domain verifiable tasks: math, code, knowledge (multiple-choice) questions, instruction following, structured outputs, and multi-step tool use in a simulated workplace environment. Although this mix contains no multi-turn conversations, it further improves multi-turn function calling.
Data composition

Gemini 4 Carbon is now available
Today, we’re making Gemini 4 Carbon available to developers, enterprises, scientists, and consumers. Carbon is our strongest model with frontier performance in cybersecurity capabilities and long-horizon agentic workflows across complex knowledge work, software engineering, and scientific reasoning.
Two weeks ago, we released Carbon to a set of cybersecurity defenders via our Fairwind Program. Following our recent launch of Gemini 4 Argon, Carbon pushes the frontier even further. Argon remains the ideal choice for the majority of software engineering and knowledge work, while Carbon is built for tasks that test the limits of a model’s intelligence like complex, multi-step coding and debugging and open-ended scientific research and discovery — using more tokens than Argon to explore thoroughly, reason deeply, and run extended verification loops.
Across independent benchmarks designed to test model performance in real workflows, Carbon pairs frontier accuracy with practical production economics. It ranks #1 on CursorBench 4.0, Perplexity’s WANDR, and Zapier’s AutomationBench at more than 2X lower cost per task compared to the next best external model.
To put Carbon’s capabilities to work on larger and complex projects, we’re previewing /swarm
in Google Antigravity, turning a single prompt into a coordinated team of agents you can track in real time. Developers can assign Carbon to roles that demand the deepest reasoning, like architectural design, coordination, and auditing, while pairing it with faster, lighter models across parallel isolated workspaces and adversarial verifiers that test every change.
Gemini 4 Carbon is available via the API in Google AI Studio and Gemini for business for all paying developers and enterprises, at the same introductory price 1 as Gemini 4 Argon ($2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens). It is also rolling out to all Google AI Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity, the Gemini app, and AI Mode in Search.
Higher-precision knowledge work, artifact generation, and data analysis
Across legal, finance, and enterprise operations, Gemini 4 Carbon combines frontier visual understanding, reasoning, and exhaustive retrieval to synthesize grounded insights across large sets of dense documents and data. It follows strict schemas and formatting to generate polished and precise spreadsheets, presentations, and reports.
Existing benchmarks don’t adequately capture how agents reason natively over dense files with charts, images, blueprints, schematics, and tables, so we partnered with Artificial Analysis to launch the new Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA) benchmark that tests a model’s multimodal performance in agentic workflows. Carbon ranks #2 while being more than 6X lower in average cost per task compared to the top performing model.
In pre-release evaluations, Carbon matched the performance of the best model tested on deep financial research on Hebbia’s E2E Financial Agentic evaluation, and ranked at the top out of 23 frontier model configurations on Balyasny Asset Management’s General Financial Intelligence benchmark, spanning legal expertise, agentic tool use and execution, coding and data engineering, and perception and context understanding.
Improved agentic coding, full stack development, and 3D and UI design
Carbon performs exceptionally well on engineering tasks that require multi-agent collaboration like multi-package migrations, cross-subsystem root-cause investigations, and complex architectural redesigns. For web app development, it runs build-and-verify loops, recovers from errors, and checks both its code and the rendered UI to produce complete, working applications. Stronger visual design, spatial reasoning, and attention to environmental detail also carry over to 3D game development and creative coding.
Frontier cybersecurity capabilities
Gemini 4 Carbon for cyber delivers our strongest cybersecurity capabilities to date, giving security teams the end-to-end intelligence they need in protecting critical software. When accessed through the Fairwind Program, Carbon leads on key benchmarks across finding (SEC-bench Pro), exploiting (ExploitGym), and patching (CWE-bench v1) vulnerabilities: inspecting software, tracing how flaws can be chained together across systems, and generating verified root-cause patches.
Early testers inside and outside of Google are already seeing strong results with Carbon for cyber in practice.
- In Project Fortify, Google’s autonomous system spanning scanning, triage, and remediation, Carbon hit 100% recall on scanning and 95% precision on triage, on our internal benchmark. On Open Source code repository testing we see an over 25% relative improvement on Argon's already strong recall rate, surfacing previously undetected, real-world logic flaws. Bringing these gains across Google, one of the world’s largest users of open-source software, helps secure both our own systems and the broader ecosystem.
- Google’s Cloud Vulnerability Research (CVR) team recently used Carbon to prove that two bugs in a popular open-source software were in fact exploitable vulnerabilities, comparable in severity to the recent PHP2Shell exploit. By using Carbon to build a proof of concept, CVR helped maintainers re-classify the bug as critical and swiftly issue a patch. Details will be shared after the responsible disclosure process completes.
- As part of Wiz’s Scan for Good program, the team used Carbon to assess vulnerabilities in public digital infrastructure. For example, when scanning two major SaaS providers, the model uncovered 0-day vulnerabilities in under two hours compressing weeks of vulnerability research to a single afternoon. The team partnered with the impacted organizations to remediate in record time, helping to mitigate potential impact on tens of thousands of companies.
Stronger scientific and mathematical reasoning
Gemini 4 Carbon shows strongly improved performance in reasoning across physics, math, and life sciences, synthesizing experimental data, testing hypotheses, and reasoning through multi-step domain problems. For drug toxicity research company Axiom Bio, Carbon is now the leading model in performance for translational science, finding novel mechanisms of toxicity they hadn’t found previously. Axiom is now moving their production scientific analyses and agents to both Carbon and Argon to unlock the creation of safer drugs.
Researchers across Google have been using Carbon in Google Antigravity to accelerate their work:
- Code verification: Researchers built a new agentic framework for formal verification called AlphaProof Code and put it to work on a major security challenge: mathematically proving the actual code underlying the cryptographic protocol of Signal. Using Carbon alongside other models, our researchers translated security goals to mathematical theorems. AlphaProof Code agents then used Carbon to generate millions of lines of code in Lean, a computer language for writing mathematical proofs, helping them prove key security properties in weeks — a task that historically takes expert teams years. The result indicates Carbon’s potential to unlock scalable formal verification, long considered a gold-standard approach to building secure software.
- Enzyme assay development: Provided with only lab notebooks and raw data, Carbon went beyond standard analysis to surface hard-to-interpret data anomalies, which it used to diagnose subtle wet lab experimental artifacts such as incomplete automated mixing in deep wells, leading to substantially improved reproducibility. Moreover Carbon improved methods to deconvolute chromatography peaks and caught trace sample carryover in research instruments, significantly accelerating the development of new assays and tightening the feedback loop between computation and the bench.
- Protein structure prediction: Structure prediction models like AlphaFold 3 use Multiple Sequence Alignments (MSAs) of evolutionary relatives to help infer how amino acid chains fold. As a result they often struggle on understudied, viral, microbial, and eukaryotic proteins that have very few matches in standard databases. Working in a multi-agent setup, our researchers used Gemini 4 Carbon to autonomously discover remote homologs across petabase-scale unannotated sequence archives, environmental and viral sequence catalogs, and 3D structure databases. For example, across 7 low-homolog protein families from the CASP17 blind test set, Carbon increased the number of homologs retrieved by 40-fold on average, greatly increasing the information available to structure prediction models without need for retraining. While broader benchmarking is still underway, addressing this upstream search bottleneck potentially offers a promising path toward modeling hard-to-characterize regions of the proteome.
Four weeks ago, we opened applications to give 10,000 scientists access to Argon in Google Antigravity free of charge for six months to accelerate the pace of their research, and we’ve onboarded thousands of scientists already. Today, we’re expanding access to Carbon for current and future participants, and going forward, the program will continue providing access to our latest frontier models as they become available. Applications remain open and onboarding continues on a weekly rolling basis, subject to eligibility, capacity, and selection.
